Our method, ADAPT (ADvisor-Aware Post-Training), is a multi-stage recipe that instills this behavior, learning entirely from the policy's own rollouts supervised by the environment's outcome, with no learned reward model or human annotation. Across three domains, compared to an untrained harness baseline, ADAPT improves success rate in embodied text reasoning (TextWorld) from 24.5% to 77.3%, code generation (LiveCodeBench) from 21.8% to 56.0%, and deep web search (GAIA) from 17.5% to 49.3%, while querying the advisor sparingly (~1.0-2.1 calls per task). On the two long-horizon domains it closes 70-85% of the gap to an oracle that perfectly times when to ask for advice, and on code generation it exceeds that oracle. The gains persist when the advisor is replaced by one unseen in training, showing that the learned help-seeking policy is robust to a changing advisor rather than tied to the one it was trained with.
comment: Published at the OE-Agent Workshop (Open and Efficient Agentic AI for Resource-Constrained Environments) at ACML 2026 14 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables

title: Breaking the Long Horizon: Short-Horizon Process Supervision for Long-Form Generation in LLMs
abstract: Long-form generation is increasingly important for agentic LLM systems, yet current reinforcement learning methods typically optimize an entire document with a single outcome-level reward. This delayed and coarse-grained supervision makes it difficult to localize errors and assign credit across semantically distinct parts of the output. To address this, we propose a short-horizon framework that reformulates long-form generation through semantic decomposition into segment-level decisions. Each segment is generated with prefix-conditioned context, allowing cross-segment coherence to be preserved while keeping supervision local. The generated segments are then scored with rubric-based rewards for adherence, coherence, and relevance, enabling explicit local supervision at the segment level. These local rewards are used to compute step-wise advantages, yielding localized policy updates. To isolate the effect of supervision granularity, we instantiate both outcome-level supervision and our short-horizon process reward method (SH-PRM) under the same GRPO framework. Across multiple LLMs and two long-form generation benchmarks, SH-PRM consistently outperforms outcome-level supervision and strong inference-time baselines under the same optimizer and comparable budgets. Further analyses suggest that these gains primarily arise from improved credit assignment. Overall, our results suggest that aligning supervision granularity with the semantic structure of long-form generation is an effective design principle for long-form LLM training.

title: $γ$-Scape: An Agent-Centric World for Mobile Embodied Intelligence
abstract: Recent embodied agents construct and adapt robot behavior through executable programs, tool use, and interaction feedback. Studying these systems in mobile manipulation calls for physical worlds that connect agent-directed execution with its physical consequences and reusable interaction experience. We introduce $γ$-Scape, an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for mobile embodied intelligence. Agents compose motion tools and learned skills to carry out complete tasks that combine navigation and manipulation in a persistent physical world. BenchForge grounds structured objectives in physical task instances with instructions, reference programs, and goal evaluators, defining task goals while preserving agents' choice of valid solutions. An agentic collection harness further enables agents to produce demonstrations by carrying out contact-rich interactions through sustained control and physical feedback. Assisted reference execution and human guidance provide complementary experience. The resulting tool traces and aligned observation-action records support program refinement and policy learning, with common task-goal criteria for subsequent evaluation. We benchmark representative agent systems on complete tasks and demonstrate contact collection and trace-informed program revision. Together, these workflows provide infrastructure for research on embodied recursive self-improvement.

title: Belief-State Management Meets Rubric Rewards for Agentic Forecasting
abstract: Current large language model (LLM) agents still struggle to forecast real-world events. This stems from two primary limitations: i) standard ReAct harness accumulates reasoning and evidence within one growing context, and ii) outcome-based rewards in forecasting lead to a slow and noisy signal that cannot distinguish sound reasoning from lucky guesses. To address these, we introduce a forecasting training framework including harness design and post-training. For the harness side, we propose Proactive Belief-State Management (PBM), equipping agents with a fold tool to compress lengthy context into compact belief states and reset the context for subsequent exploration. For the training side, we develop SEIPH, a five-dimensional, outcome-blind rubric, providing process-quality rewards. Using the rubric-based reward, we post-train a 35B model with PPO and GRPO, yielding DeepForecaster-PPO and DeepForecaster-GRPO. Theoretically, we prove that idealized fold-based stopping converges and calibrated local rewards reduce segment-level gradient variance. Empirically, DeepForecaster-PPO (35B) achieves the best Brier score on both ForecastBench and Polymarket-Sim, outperforming frontier agents based on DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T), Kimi-K2.6 (1T), and GPT-5.5. DeepForecaster-GRPO ranks second on both FutureX metrics. Ablations reveal that PBM also improves the untrained base model without any training. Calibration analysis shows that DeepForecaster-PPO makes more accurate high-confidence predictions than Qwen3.6 and GPT-5.5. Trajectory analysis further shows that forecasts generally improve from the first to the final belief state as agents gather evidence and revise their judgments.

title: SIR-Agent: Skill-Augmented Image Restoration Agent with Recursive Self-Improvement
abstract: Agents for Image Restoration (IR) aim to leverage Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to autonomously perceive image degradation and invoke IR tools. However, existing IR agents typically rely on fine-tuning MLLM parameters to adapt to new IR tasks, leading to catastrophic forgetting of IR knowledge. To address this limitation, we propose a skill-augmented IR agent, dubbed SIR-Agent, that maintains IR knowledge in a scalable skill library and uses Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) to facilitate efficient skill-library evolution. Specifically, we design a Chain Feedback-driven Skill Revision (CFSR) to evolve the skill library. The CFSR analyzes restoration chains to identify and revise weak operations in existing skills. The compatibility of a revised skill with known tasks decides if it replaces the original skill or is appended independently. Furthermore, to advance CFSR's skill-library evolution, we present an RSI-driven skill meta-learning mechanism, which identifies CFSR's inefficient operations and autonomously refines its revision strategy. Extensive experiments across 14 IR benchmarks, covering 6 single-degradation and 8 mixed-degradation scenarios, demonstrate SIR-Agent's superior IR performance. Further evaluation on 7 unseen tasks validates SIR-Agent's generalization to new IR tasks.

title: When Students Fail to Learn from Teachers: Learning Dynamics of On-Policy Distillation
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a core technique for post-training large language models, enabling students to learn from dense token-level supervision on their own generations. However, even with a capable teacher, OPD training can be unstable, leading to excessive response length, repetitive generation, and severe performance degradation. One example is \textit{spurious agreement}, where the student maintains high overlap with the teacher at the states visited but produces repetitive generations. Although such failures have been observed, the mechanisms behind these failures remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we investigate OPD through the lens of learning dynamics, tracing three mechanisms from local analysis to subsequent on-policy sampling. We first identify states where sampled-token OPD updates fail to correct teacher--student mismatch and characterize them using the student's mass on the teacher's top-$p$ set. We then show that learning from the teacher is difficult at mismatched states and that their gradients can also affect with learning at other tokens. Finally, using a termination-token mismatch as a case study, we study how continued training on mismatched states influences on-policy sampling, suppressing the student's current modes and leading the student toward states where the teacher is unreliable . These findings help explain the benefits of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization and motivate targeted correction of states where student and teacher are mismatched.

title: CTRL: Concurrent Training and Rollout for LLM Reinforcement Learning via GPU Co-Residency
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models runs two GPU workloads with different hardware demands: rollout decoding, which is dominated by memory access and whose batch shrinks as responses finish, and a dense learner. Current systems either time-share every GPU between them, paying serial phases and switches, or split GPUs into pools whose sizes change only in whole devices. We present CTRL, which makes co-residency a third RL execution layout: every GPU runs a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine, sharing the device under CUDA MPS. A host-owned learner makes the layout fit: optimizer state stays in host memory, and policy weights stream layer by layer through a bounded GPU window. A publication gate trains each ready batch first and waits only before releasing the next policy, keeping a dropless staleness bound. A step-time bound guides compute-share selection, and a GPU-time ledger explains overlap and sharing costs. On H100, A800, and RTX 4090 GPUs with Qwen3 models, CTRL achieves 1.11-2.24$\times$ the throughput of the stronger of verl's asynchronous baselines across 24 workload settings with the staleness limit set to two, and 1.23$\times$ verl's colocate_async on eight H100 GPUs. With the same learner, co-residency is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than time-sharing on all three platforms and 1.10-1.30$\times$ faster than the best measured whole-GPU split on H100 DAPO-Math workloads at 256-528 trajectories per step, on four and eight GPUs.

title: CoEvoBench: Can LLMs Drive Recursive Co-Evolution of Agentic Systems?
abstract: The performance of an LLM agent depends on both its model and its harness, the code that mediates its interaction with tools and environments. Can LLM researchers drive this co-evolution as a recursive improvement process, deciding round after round which component to change when each change alters the value of the other? Existing benchmarks evaluate post-training or data research with the harness out of scope, or harness optimization with the model fixed, leaving this joint decision unmeasured. We introduce CoEvoBench, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs as researchers co-evolving the model and harness of a target agent across five agentic domains. Researchers start from a common base model and initial harness, train and revise within a 24-hour budget, and submit a model-harness pair that is scored on separate test tasks. Across five frontier researchers, the strongest closes more than four fifths of the gap to an instruction-tuned reference system, and co-evolution succeeds on interaction tasks but rarely on long-horizon coding. These results suggest that current LLMs can make a strong first improvement, but cannot yet turn feedback from an improved system into the next one. CoEvoBench provides a controlled testbed for measuring the research capabilities that recursive co-evolution requires.

title: RemoteEvolver: Expanding Earth Observation Capabilities through Agent Harness Evolution
abstract: We are interested in developing a continually self-improving remote sensing agentic system. It should identify and address its capability gaps, retaining the resulting improvements to enhance performance on subsequent tasks. However, existing systems typically rely on fixed toolsets and confine their experience accumulation to re-orchestrating predefined capabilities, constraining both capability expansion and the transfer of improvements across tasks. As the infrastructure for agentic systems, the harness manages tools and workflow knowledge as editable, persistent resources outside the base model. These resources can therefore be updated and reused across tasks without additional post-training. Based on these observations, we propose RemoteEvolver, an external harness for remote sensing agents that drives tool and workflow evolution through execution feedback. With the base model parameters fixed, RemoteEvolver acquires missing specialized tools on demand and distills verified successful execution experience from individual tasks into agent skills that can be reused across tasks. The acquired tools and accumulated skills jointly support planning and execution on subsequent tasks. Experiments on Earth-Bench and OpenEarthAgent-Bench show that RemoteEvolver achieves average accuracy gains of 8.18 and 23.86 percentage points over its initial state when tools are fully available and partially missing. Under the same settings, it also outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by an average of 6.77 and 17.10 percentage points, respectively.

title: Decision Models Are General-Purpose Process Reward Models
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) from verifiable outcomes gives a language agent one reward per episode: every step is credited alike, and nothing about the task is learned when all rollouts fail. The last mile, step-level credit, usually requires step labels, a learned critic, costly LLM judges or hand-written rules. We introduce DM-PRM, which turns a general-purpose decision model -- one answering yes/no questions with probabilities -- into a general-purpose process reward model (PRM), zero-shot: no step labels, no fine-tuning, no critic. DM-PRM asks one question per step and adds the standardised answers to the advantage. It plugs into any policy-gradient method; one model, with one question text per environment, serves household tasks, web shopping and multiple RL methods. With Qwen2.5-1.5B it lifts GRPO by over twenty points on ALFWorld and over ten on WebShop, overtakes GiGPO on ALFWorld and learns in far fewer iterations; it also improves GiGPO and GraphGPO on both benchmarks and reaches the highest success of our comparison, ahead of critic-based PPO and of state-of-the-art GiGPO, HGPO and GraphGPO. Its scores locate useful steps in failed rollouts, and trained agents drop idle actions and explore instead of circling. DM-PRM shows that step credit need not be learned: it can be asked for.

title: Physics-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement of Amortized Bayesian Inference Across Physics
abstract: Across physics, from the orbits of imaged exoplanets and the matter inside neutron stars to thin films at synchrotrons and cortical neurons, conservation laws, interference, and compensating currents compress the posteriors of precise data into tiny, curved regions where Markov chains need minutes to days. We introduce PhyRSI (physics-guided recursive self-improvement), in which an AI agent coupled to the simulator writes and revises an amortized Bayesian inference algorithm for each field, scored by the importance weights of the exact likelihood because the true posterior is unknown. It evolves coordinates, symmetries, and factorizations matched to the physics: orbital elements at the best-measured epoch, Fresnel-normalized reflectivity with a chart for each of its multiple solutions, coordinates along which Na+ and K+ currents compensate, a shared neutron-star equation of state that factorizes a 32-dimensional joint analysis, and the time-rescaling symmetry of predator-prey dynamics. In six fields, networks trained once on simulations return 36 posteriors of real observations in seconds, reweighted by the likelihood and agreeing with converged Markov chains about as closely as two independent chains agree with each other. Such posteriors could steer synchrotron film growth and patch-clamp recordings as they run, follow X-ray transients while they are bright, update the dense-matter equation of state as neutron stars are added, and compare physical models across catalogs. Inference can thus be evolved and checked by the physics itself rather than designed by hand for each problem.

title: Reward Integrity in Adversarial Reinforcement Learning for LLM Guardrail Red-Teaming
abstract: We study reward fidelity in an adversarial reinforcement-learning loop for red-teaming financial-services language-model guardrails. Apparent wins can arise when an attack omits prescribed personally identifiable information (PII), or when a reward judge credits a response that did not break the targeted policy. On attacker-generated and public benchmark examples, TypeSafe Jev checks whether the prescribed PII is present. For outcome scoring, we compare the decision models TypeSafe Jev, Laya (pretrained and post-trained), and pretrained CLM-8B with logged Opus 4.8 judgements from a replay corpus. Post-training markedly improves Laya's agreement with the judge. A separate author-reviewed off-target set establishes that Opus can award false wins. The findings motivate specialised decision-model judges for checking prescribed PII in attack inputs and scoring target responses against the intended policy.
comment: Received the Best Paper Award at the Reinforcement Learning for LLM Agents Workshop at ACM International Conference for AI in Finance 2026 in Milan

title: Self-Evolving Beyond Human-Crafted Experience for EDA Scripting
abstract: The growing complexity of electronic systems demands efficient design flows, yet EDA scripting remains a bottleneck: proprietary APIs are sparsely documented, and errors often appear as silent failures or cryptic exceptions. Hand-crafted knowledge helps but is difficult to maintain as toolchains evolve. We present ZhuLong-SE (Self-Evolution), an execution-grounded LLM agent that learns reusable knowledge from prior task traces. Building on ZhuLong, it enhances the task-level harness with API retrieval, documentation responses, isolated sandbox execution, and static checking, then adds governed cross-task self-evolution. Beyond solving individual tasks, ZhuLong-SE distills past execution traces into a three-tier memory store governed by ground-truth anchoring, disconfirmation filtering, held-out rollback, and anti-leakage retrieval. On the 158-task EDA-Eval-PyAether benchmark, the full task-level harness, with self-evolution disabled, achieves 92.4% pass@1 and outperforms ZhuLong on all five tested LLM backbones. On a harder instance-disjoint test set, self-evolution from the bare configuration surpasses a human-crafted-experience baseline by 2.5 percentage points (80.0% vs. 77.5% pass@1).
comment: Submitted to DATE 2027. 7 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables

title: AstronautBench: Measuring Agent Self-Improvement Across Episodes Through Knowledge, Evidence, and Progress
abstract: LLM agents are expected to improve themselves from their own experience across episodes, with fixed weights. Self-improvement in an embodied world cannot be read from one measure. Existing benchmarks measure task progress, world-knowledge question answering (QA), and episodic memory, but a correct answer does not show that the agent ever observed the evidence for it, and progress does not show what the agent learned. We introduce AstronautBench, which measures one agent's self-improvement through three views on the same run: what it knows, whether its own evidence supports that knowledge, and how far it gets in the world. It is built on the game Outer Wilds, where each episode is a 22-minute loop after which the world resets, only the agent's knowledge carries over, and progress is gated by knowledge. After every episode, we measure the places reached and ship-log rumor facts revealed, the correctness of answers to 164 questions about the world, and whether each answer is supported by the frames and position the agent cites from its own recorded play. Two LLM judges from different model families check every answer. In eight-episode baselines with GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon planners, which act through a learned controller or their own gamepad inputs, the three views do not move together, so any one of them alone gives an incomplete picture of whether the agent is improving. The GPT-6.1 Sol agent's correct answers grow from 14.6% to 26.8% of all questions, but at episode 8 only 59 to 68% of them are supported by its cited evidence. It reveals no new rumor facts after episode 3, while the places it reaches and its memory keep growing. More than half of the answers that become correct after episode 3 cite only evidence from earlier episodes.

title: MedicalRSI: Medical Recursive Self-Improving Agents via Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution
abstract: Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We propose MedicalRSI, an RSI framework built on Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution, in which one model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent itself, and the Improver is its learnable improving strategy, which writes a medical harness from the agent's failures. Each harness is rewarded by its gain over acting without it, and both roles are trained together, so the Improver keeps adapting to the problems the Solver has not yet solved. On multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, MedicalRSI outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods and transfers well to unseen workflows, new LLMs and new databases, a step toward medical agents that keep improving.

title: Spatial Query Execution as Verifiable Rewards for Multi-step Spatial Reasoning
abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) remain unreliable on spatial reasoning problems that require composing grounded relations across multiple objects. Yet, scaling reasoning supervision is challenging since human-annotated visual datasets often rely on fixed relational annotations and coarse object localization, making it difficult to obtain precise intermediate reasoning states across diverse spatial configurations and complexities. We introduce FARON (Fully Automated Reasoning Over spatial relatioNs), a framework that executes spatial queries to provide both execution-grounded reasoning supervision and verifiable outcome rewards. Rather than relying on existing annotated data, FARON constructs synthetic 2D and 3D scenes with explicit geometries, enabling configurable object arrangements, spatial relations, and multi-step compositions. Deterministic query execution yields intermediate sets and final answers, providing precise supervision without manual relation annotation. Our pipeline converts intermediate states into natural-language reasoning traces for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while the execution-derived answers provide verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Controlled experiments show that trace-based SFT improves multi-step spatial reasoning over final-answer supervision and that subsequent group relative policy optimization (GRPO) provides further gains. The resulting models also demonstrate transfer across external spatial reasoning benchmarks and multiple LVLM backbones without benchmark-specific fine-tuning. These results show the potential of using spatial query execution as a unified, flexible source of reasoning supervision and verifiable outcome rewards for multimodal spatial reasoning.

title: ACE-Brain-0.7: Learning Execution-Grounded Reasoning for Embodied Agents
abstract: Reliable reasoning for long-horizon embodied tasks requires predictions grounded in the observed execution state. We present ACE-Brain-0.7, a 9B vision--language model that combines spatial grounding, task understanding, and progress estimation. To train the model, we curate 3.7 million question--answer pairs, drawing execution supervision from egocentric human videos, robot episodes, and simulation. These questions span different stages of an execution and connect task-level judgments with observed progress and outcomes. We then fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this collection together with additional task, spatial-grounding, and progress-estimation data. Across six public task-reasoning benchmarks, ACE-Brain-0.7 achieves an average score of 76.5, ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 72.7 and Claude Opus 5.5 at 73.5. Our model also leads the evaluated models in spatial grounding, averaging 75.90 across seven benchmarks and reaching 91.25 Acc@0.5 on RefCOCOg. Controlled evaluations further indicate that our task-only model makes more effective use of visual history and more accurately distinguishes execution states. Together, these results show that ACE-Brain-0.7 effectively combines spatial perception with temporal understanding, delivering strong execution-grounded reasoning and comparing favorably with closed-source models.

title: Training LLMs to Follow Reasoning Instructions with Minimal Edits
abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on extended reasoning traces, yet the training signals used to shape this behavior remain coarse. Supervised fine-tuning on full trajectories forces the model to imitate an entire demonstration, overconstraining its output distribution, while trajectory-level reinforcement learning provides only weak credit assignment, rewarding or penalizing whole completions without identifying where they succeed or fail. We propose edit-based training, a general framework for learning from a model's own trajectories via localized textual corrections. Given a sampled completion, an editor identifies the first point of failure under a specified criterion and proposes a minimal replacement span. The model is then supervised only on these edited spans. By design, this concentrates supervision where the model's reasoning first breaks down and aims to preserve its existing reasoning patterns elsewhere. The method applies both offline and online, with the latter continually adapting supervision to the model's evolving failure modes. We instantiate this approach on reasoning instruction following with Qwen3-32B on the ReasonIF benchmark. Compared to full-trajectory imitation and trajectory-level reinforcement learning baselines, edit-based training substantially improves compliance with the reasoning instruction while largely preserving the model's skills on untargeted tasks. These results suggest that localized correction is an effective complement to these approaches for shaping how LLMs reason.
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Transitioning from Pre-training to Post-training

title: Sage-Evolve-Preview:Adaptive Observation for Post-Training Self-Improvement
abstract: Post-training recursive self-improvement (RSI) iteratively improves a target capability, operationalized by a fixed anchor benchmark, through repeated intervention, training, and evaluation. Yet most loops use the anchor's aggregate score as their sole observation, so early gains give way to stalled progress and repetitive exploration. When this anchor-only feedback ceases to reveal actionable gaps, a plateau may reflect an exhausted observation rather than an exhausted capability. We introduce adaptive observation (AdaObs), an observation-side mechanism of harness evolution that keeps the anchor objective fixed while adapting the active observation. At a plateau, a controller refines diagnostic granularity, escalates difficulty, and adds related tasks; validated increments are fused back into training, while every checkpoint remains evaluated against the anchor. Across eight independently optimized anchors in long-context reading comprehension and instruction following, AdaObs raises the mean score from $66.4$ to $73.7$ under a matched data budget, outperforming FixedObs, the anchor-only baseline. The evolved harness further improves the seven-task average on the independent PostTrainBench across two agent backends. These results identify observation adaptation as a missing mechanism of harness evolution for sustaining post-training RSI.

title: RL Can Only Reinforce What It Sees Succeed
abstract: When a familiar rule stops working, an agent has to weigh what pre-training taught it against what it now observes. We ask how outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL) changes this balance, in a puzzle world where both sides are known: small language models trained from scratch on games played by a Bayesian player, so that the prior and the right answer are exact. Base models hedge as their corpus did, and RL turns that hedging into decisions, in whichever direction the reward favours. But RL can only reinforce what it sees succeed. When the right action is rare, each run either learns it everywhere or not at all, and which runs take off is predicted before training by one count: the expected number of groups of attempts in which the action wins. About 35 such groups give even odds. The count holds for new and repeated problems and for groups of 4 to 256 attempts, and across learning rates, optimizers, GRPO variants and model sizes from 1.3M to 85M parameters, which move the threshold but not what is counted.

title: System-One RSI: Building Muscle Memory for Interactive Agents through Guided Practice
abstract: Reasoning models provide strong multimodal task understanding but struggle with sub-second control because deliberation increases decision latency. Fast decision models can meet the response window, yet prompting and few-shot examples do not readily provide the fine-grained experience required by a new task. Inspired by coached motor learning, this paper presents System-One Recursive Self-Improvement (System-One RSI), which couples two loops. The high-frequency online inner loop is an Observe, Orient, Decide, Act (OODA) cycle: a decision model maps each visual observation and task question to structured judgments, and a decision tree converts them into timed actions without invoking a reasoning model. The offline outer loop is a recursive improvement cycle carried out by a team of reasoning agents. The team revises the decision-model prompt and decision tree, captures interaction records, derives supervision from those records, and trains or deploys updated model parameters. The improved system then returns to the environment and generates the experience for the next round, consolidating learned distinctions as external muscle memory. The framework operates with a small number of real episodes, without expert demonstrations, environment modification, sandboxing, or parallel simulation. Experiments in Snake, Zenless Zone Zero, and Black Myth: Wukong use a 27B decision model. Mean Snake score increases from 1.30 to 7.35. In an evaluated scenario of Zenless Zone Zero, median completion time decreases by 8.4%. In an evaluated combat scenario of Black Myth: Wukong, the evasive policy achieves 11 times the mean survival time of a stationary reference, while the offensive policy win rate rises from 0% to 66.7% across the evaluated configurations.

title: Policy Improvement-Guided Replay for Continual Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires models to acquire new capabilities while retaining performance on previous tasks. A stability-oriented perspective common in conventional continual learning emphasizes knowledge preservation and interference mitigation. Complementing this perspective, we revisit CRL for vision-language models through policy improvement, a fundamental principle of RL, to preserve acquired performance gains. Using the performance difference lemma, we characterize historical performance changes through the current policy's expected advantages on historical task distributions, motivating replay of historical prompts with the current policy. To allocate limited replay memory, we propose Contrastive Likelihood Replay (CoLiR), which contrasts likelihood gains on correct responses from the final task policy with likelihood reductions on incorrect responses from the initial policy. Our analysis links correct-response likelihood gains to reference-policy advantages under an idealized KL-regularized optimal update and provides an endogenous-reward interpretation for general policy updates. CoLiR estimates scores from finite training rollouts and cached log-likelihoods, selects prompts at task boundaries, and replays them uniformly during subsequent training, with KL regularization restricted to replayed prompts. Memory construction only requires a small amount of additional cross-policy scoring but no additional response generation. Across three Qwen3-VL model sizes on MRCL, CoLiR achieves the highest mean final accuracy and mean task accuracy among the compared methods while maintaining competitive new-task performance.

title: ROAM-GRPO: Enforcing Reasoning Diversity in GRPO via Routed Off-mode Approach Mining
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paired with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become the dominant recipe for post-training LLMs on complex reasoning tasks, but has been shown to collapse the policy into a low-diversity mode. Repeated LLM outputs are nearly identical, and pass@k accuracy converges or degrades as a result. We propose ROAM-GRPO (Routed Off-mode Approach Mining for GRPO), an augmentation to the GRPO algorithm which incentivizes exploration of distinct reasoning strategies and aims to increase output creativity during evaluation. ROAM-GRPO detects well-solved problems during training and transfers them to an "off-mode" track. The model is prompted to produce distinct solution strategies to such problems, which are verified for logical validity and distinctness by an LLM judge and subsequently self-distilled into the policy. Training Qwen3.5-2b on a 1,000-problem subset of the MATH lvl5 dataset, ROAM-GRPO implementation increases peak pass@16 by 4.7 percentage points and correct embedding cosine distance by approximately 1.5-2x on a difficult evaluation set.
comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Transitioning from Pre-Training to Post-Training Workshop

title: Meta-RTL: Evolving Agent Harnesses for RTL Optimization
abstract: Large language models enable agents to optimize RTL using EDA feedback, yet their executable search procedures remain largely hand- engineered. We present Meta-RTL, an EDA-grounded framework that evolves RTL optimization harnesses from a minimal loop while keeping the optimization model, EDA flow, and per-design budgets fixed. Compared with Dr. RTL, Meta-RTL* reduces aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 7.8%/11.0% across 20 development designs, with area reductions on 70% of them. Without further evolution, Meta-RTL* transfers to 10 unseen IC-RTL designs, reducing aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 20.5%/14.0% and total synthesized area by 12.6%. We further characterize three search mechanisms in the evolved harness and assess their contributions through ablations and a case study.

title: Goal-Guided Reinforcement Learning via Fine-Tuning Vision-Language Models
abstract: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons. Large language models (LLMs) can guide exploration by generating high-level goals, but methods using models without explicit task adaptation often rely on carefully designed prompts and may produce inconsistent or contextually inappropriate goals. We introduce CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset constructed from interaction trajectories in Craftax-Classic, and propose a vision-language model (VLM)-guided RL framework that learns environment-specific goal guidance from this dataset. The framework consists of two stages: offline VLM fine-tuning and online goal-guided RL. In the offline stage, we align the VLM with goal preferences using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. Experiments on Craftax-Classic show that our method collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines, achieves the highest score and reward, and attains the highest success rates on most achievements.

title: CompAct-Bench: A Benchmark for Working-Context Compaction in Long-Horizon Agent Tasks
abstract: As language-model agents are applied to increasingly extended tasks, their working context continuously accumulates interaction history, tool observations, intermediate decisions, and task progress. Context compaction offers a practical way to reduce this growing history while allowing execution to continue, yet the compaction ability of modern LLMs remains insufficiently understood. We introduce CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction through its downstream effect on agent task completion. Starting from successful agent trajectories, we insert compaction boundaries at different stages of execution, compress the preceding working context with the model under evaluation, and let the same executor continue the original task. To enable fair comparison across compactors, we evaluate them under controlled retention ratios using a lightweight iterative ratio-adjustment procedure. CompAct-Bench covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks through BrowseComp, SWE-bench, and an internal CompanyBench evaluation. Our experiments show that working-context compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models: Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, yet substantial degradation in downstream task accuracy persists under aggressive compaction. Further analysis reveals that failures are often caused not only by omitted information, but also by distorted task state, such as turning unresolved issues into apparent conclusions or forgetting previously established results, which can lead to incorrect decisions or redundant execution. These findings highlight working-context compaction as a distinct and still challenging ability for LLMs operating in extended agent tasks.

title: Cyber-Physical RSI for AI-RAN: A Case Study
abstract: Learned models for radio access networks (RANs) are often developed using simulation, yet their predictions can shift when exposed to physical propagation conditions, protocol behavior, and equipment implementations. This paper presents a cyber-physical recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework for AI-RAN that connects a task-oriented student model, an experiment-planning coach agent, a calibratable virtual environment, and a physical host agent. Physical measurements are organized as evidence for both model adaptation and subsequent experiment planning. We examine an implementation of the physical-feedback pathway using ping-pong handover as a case study. The system completes 12 physical executions organized into six baseline--candidate pairs, updates the student from measured outcomes, and evaluates the revised model on reserved physical configurations. In the observed short-window tests, increasing the time-to-trigger from 320 to 1280\,ms changes the ping-pong count from three to zero. The updated student achieves a grouped-validation mean absolute error (MAE) of 2.673 round trips/min, while a common three-configuration physical evaluation yields MAEs of 1.240 and 1.601 round trips/min for the pre-feedback and post-feedback models, respectively. These results characterize both the operational feedback loop and the parameter-dependent generalization behavior revealed by new physical experiments.

title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.

title: Decision-Focused Reinforcement Learning for LLM Post-Training
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as predictors across various tasks, benefiting from their ability to use information from unstructured context. However, when predictions serve as parameters of downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not necessarily translate into lower decision costs. We propose decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), a framework for post-training LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as reward. DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize the costs of the decisions induced by their predictions, without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, and integrates readily into existing RL post-training frameworks. To address expensive reward evaluation, we develop two approaches. Heuristic warm-starting uses inexpensive approximate rewards during an initial phase before switching to refinement with exact rewards. Reward correction combines inexpensive estimates with randomized exact evaluations, preserving the expected policy gradient while reducing the expected number of exact solves per update. Experiments on three synthetic optimization problems demonstrate improvements over prediction-loss baselines, while a larger knapsack experiment shows faster early improvement under short training budgets. On inventory planning with H&M transactions and product descriptions, our best configuration, in which the LLM reasons before predicting, reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the SFT baseline and 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.

title: SegAnyFruit: Learning Generalizable and Edge Deployable Fruit Instance Segmentation at Scale
abstract: Deploying fruit instance segmentation in real agricultural settings requires generalizing across unseen species, orchards, and imaging conditions under strict onboard compute and annotation budgets. We introduce SegAnyFruit (SAF), a data construction and progressive training framework that distills foundation-model priors into lightweight, prompt-free segmenters. SAF combines generic mask pre-training, broad mid-training on automatically annotated web imagery from our curated WebFruits dataset, and human-verified agricultural refinement post-training on PaperFruits, together spanning 733K images and 9.66M whole-fruit masks across 165 fruit types. Across seven benchmarks, zero-shot SAF-RF-DETR-XL reaches 69.06 average mask AP50:95 (+4.76 over SAM 3) while remaining deployable on edge devices. SAF initialization also boosts few-shot to full-shot adaptation across five agricultural domains while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Finally, we systematically analyze training stages, data scale, model capacity, and generative augmentation, and validate our pipeline's transferability to underwater, cell, and human segmentation. We will release our datasets, code, and SAF models.

title: Evolve Where It Matters: Coverage-Guided Self-Evolution of Agent Skills
abstract: Agent skills package procedural knowledge as natural-language instructions, and a skill helps only when its instructions are correct and properly followed by the agent. Self-evolving agents revise their own skills from the runs they make, but existing methods judge each run as a whole, by its outcome or by where it went wrong, and cannot tell whether a failure comes from a wrong instruction or from one the agent did not follow. Instruction-level coverage was introduced to test skills and labels each instruction of a run as follow, not-follow, or not covered, which separates these causes. We leverage it for skill self-evolution with SkillPlumber, a framework in which an agent evolves its own skills where coverage shows they fall short. A persistent root cause analysis agent turns each label into a revision question and checks each revision against the next run, while a maintainer distills investigations across tasks into a shared strategy library. Across three benchmarks and three executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7% to 70.5% of the tasks, 25.6 to 30.4 percentage points higher than the initial skill and 8.7 to 14.0 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline, and removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.

title: HOPD: Historical On-Policy Distillation for SAR MLLM Continual Learning
abstract: Continual SAR interpretation requires multimodal large language models to learn incoming sources while retaining earlier task abilities. This is difficult when acquisition and geographic shifts alter visual evidence, regionally concentrated categories bias answers, and historical images are scarce. We address this problem with Historical On-Policy Distillation (HOPD), which reuses source-acquisition LoRA states as persistent teachers for one evolving student. Archiving each state before consolidation preserves a stable source reference. The teachers supervise student-generated prefixes, transferring historical behavior to the student's changing generation contexts. To enrich sparse replay, original-view teachers guide augmented historical student views while preserving spatial coordinates. This knowledge is consolidated into a single deployed adapter that requires no source identity. On SARVQA-CL, our source-incremental evaluation protocol, HOPD achieves the highest final mean score of 54.51 among the compared methods, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.96 points. It also improves the final source-macro score in every evaluated task over shared-memory Replay-SFT, with gains across source orders. These results support source-acquisition history as supervision for retaining earlier task performance during continual SAR adaptation. Code and data: https://github.com/zcablii/HOPD.

title: Zero to Four Views: Unified Panorama Generation and Preference RL for Unobserved Regions
abstract: Panoramas can serve as shared scene backgrounds for multi-shot video generation, but most existing panorama generators take text alone or a single input image. We present a single model that generates a full equirectangular panorama from a text caption and K in {0,...,4} perspective conditioning views taken by a four-camera rig at one viewpoint. We fine-tune a pretrained text-to-image rectified-flow transformer in two stages. In the first stage, each conditioning view is appended to the token sequence together with the ID of its camera slot, and the number of views varies during training, so one set of weights serves every input setting. In the second stage, we improve the region not covered by any conditioning view. Supervised training computes its loss on noisy latents of the ground truth and never scores a panorama the model has generated and decoded, so we propose Uncovered-Region GRPO (UR-GRPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that rewards the candidates a vision-language model prefers in pairwise comparisons on crops around this region. Because the slot ID alone does not tell the model which way the rig points, we also offer an optional variant that writes each view's camera direction into its position encoding, which lets the user decide where each view appears in the output. With one conditioning view, our model outperforms the previous state of the art, 360Anything, trained on the same data and evaluated with the same code, on Laval Indoor and gives mixed results on an indoor subset of SUN360; the second stage improves the results for every number of conditioning views.

title: Beyond Weight Updates: Evolving Agent Harnesses for Domain Specialization
abstract: Domain specialization of LLM agents is usually framed as a weight-update problem: collect trajectories, run reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and deploy a new checkpoint. We study a complementary axis: evolving the \textbf{agent harness}---the system prompt, tool schemas, skill library, and planning scaffolding---while keeping the policy frozen. We cast harness evolution as an RL-style outer loop and instantiate it with GEPA, a reflective evolutionary optimizer. The resulting harness adapters require no GPU training, are loadable per vertical domain, and compose with weight-based RL. Experiments with Codev, a Claude Code-style coding agent, on SWE-bench Verified, OfficeBench, and Terminal-Bench show a consistent pattern: weight updates give the strongest single-path gains, harness evolution recovers most of those gains at a small fraction of the compute, and combining both paths is best overall. We also analyze a failure mode of SFT-based specialization---shortened reasoning chains and increased truncation---and argue that harness adapters avoid it by construction. Our results position harness evolution as a practical, non-destructive complement to weight updates for vertical agents.

title: Inhabitant: An Agent Framework for Long-Horizon Human-Scene Interaction with Spatial Control and Quantitative Feedback
abstract: Recent work on human-scene interaction (HSI) generation moves from single interactions to long-horizon interaction, where a language-model agent plans and executes a sequence of interactions in a 3D scene under one instruction. However, existing agents struggle in challenging everyday scenarios (e.g., picking up a toy and throwing it into a basket) because they lack spatial control over the motion and quantitative feedback on its execution, and they often fail to complete the interaction sequence. To address these gaps, we present Inhabitant, a training-free agent framework in which the agent specifies each motion through positions, paths and poses, measures how the executed interaction deviates from its intent, and revises the control specification accordingly. For an extensive evaluation in such scenarios, we build Inhabit, a benchmark of 75 household tasks in 31 furniture layouts of an apartment, in which every task chains one to three goals on movable objects and is carried out by the whole body, excluding fingers. On Inhabit, Inhabitant completes 98.7\% of the tasks with Claude Opus 5.5, and 93.3\% and 82.7\% with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, respectively. Ablations confirm that without spatial control the agent fails most tasks, and without quantitative feedback its motion becomes less precise. Code is available on the project page.

title: Vibe-Trading: Towards Agent-Native Trading
abstract: Existing AI agents can retrieve information, call tools, run experiments, and produce multi-step outputs. Yet most are built around relatively static workflows and struggle to preserve reliable state as the environment changes. Financial trading makes this limitation especially consequential: prices, news, market conditions, portfolio positions, and available capital evolve continuously. A result is useful only when it remains tied to the correct time, data snapshot, and execution context. We present Vibe-Trading, a comprehensive agent-native trading framework and all-in-one workspace for building, evaluating, and evolving agents for financial trading. It unifies market research, financial data, strategy generation, backtesting, portfolio analysis, paper trading, multi-agent collaboration, and optional broker execution. Its central contribution is an architecture that keeps results, evidence, research history, and trading authority connected throughout the research-to-action process. Each result retains its source, temporal scope, configuration, and producing run. Shared evidence grounding enables verification, versioned research records support reproducible continuation, and an explicit authority gate separates strategy research from live execution. Together, these designs provide a practical foundation for trading agents whose results can be traced, reproduced, and acted on only under explicit authority.
comment: Technical report. 16 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Code: https://github.com/HKUDS/Vibe-Trading

title: When Does Continual Pre-Training Help? A Controlled Study of Dialectal Adaptation for Québec French
abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) is widely used to adapt pretrained language models to dialectal and non-standard language varieties, yet it remains unclear when this additional training is necessary, what drives its benefits, and whether aggregate evaluation scores adequately capture its effects. In this paper, we present a controlled study of CPT for Québec French language understanding across nine LLMs spanning different families and scales. Using a budget-matched protocol of 30M tokens per experiment, our results show that the benefit of CPT depends strongly on the starting model's existing competence in the target variety. When CPT is beneficial, the improvements are driven more by corpus composition than by data volume, with literary text accounting for most of the gain. Paired Québec and standard French evaluations further show that CPT primarily improves expression comprehension rather than grammatical competence, and that corpus register determines which regional expressions are acquired. These gains also involve capability-specific trade-offs, including declines in reading comprehension that aggregate scores can conceal. Overall, these findings show that CPT for dialectal adaptation should not be treated as a uniformly beneficial default. Instead, adaptation strategies should begin with a careful assessment of the base model's existing competence, accompanied by source-level data analysis and task-level evaluation.

title: Depth Before Breadth: Reverse-to-Forward Curriculum with Advantage Decomposition for LLM Agent
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, learning from sparse terminal rewards makes credit assignment and exploration difficult. We approach these challenges through a policy-induced capability region, the set of states from which the current policy can reliably complete a task. Near its boundary, an agent may need only a few actions to reach a more solvable state, even when the goal remains distant. This reduces long-horizon learning to two coupled subproblems of reaching that state and completing the task from there. We address them with paired advantages and a progressive reverse-to-forward curriculum. The advantages provide separate signals for reaching more solvable states and completing the task from them, while the curriculum expands the capability region backward along successful reference trajectories and then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration. On ALFWorld and WebShop, our method outperforms competitive agentic RL methods at both model scales, achieving success rates of 90.1%/96.1% and 80.2%/82.6% with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, respectively.

title: Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data through Recursive Self-Improvement
abstract: We present Piccolo, a family of multimodal decision models (0.8B to 27B) that coevolves model capabilities and training data via Agentic Data Engineering and recursive self-improvement (RSI). The models predict probabilities over candidate answers for general-purpose text and visual judgments, agent harnesses, data workflows, and interactive games. Piccolo-27B tops the Decision Index Vision Full leaderboard with a score of 75.59, while Piccolo-9B and Piccolo-4B achieve 68.35 and 67.46, respectively. All three rank first on the Private benchmark in their respective model-size categories. Research agents analyze model behavior, construct training data, conduct experiments, and use the results to refine subsequent proposals. Semantic slices and a shared research memory connect these actions across the model family's development. With training recipes comprising hundreds of thousands of examples, data selection and feedback-driven refinement are central to the self-improvement process. Our large-scale RSI exploration yields three counter-intuitive insights for decision-model development: (1) Backbone-recipe co-adaptation outweighs raw model recency: earlier backbones can surpass newer generations on visual tasks under identical recipes; (2) Targeted data curation enables 4B-9B models to rival 27B baselines on specialized workflows; and (3) Continuous loss reduction can decouple from and even degrade discrete decision accuracy. Together with the released weights and tools from the Data-Juicer and AgentScope ecosystems, Piccolo provides an actionable blueprint for building frontier decision models and scaling data-driven RSI.
comment: 22 pages, 13 figures, 11 tables. Project page and blog: https://decisionplayground.agentscope.io/piccolo.html

title: Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models
abstract: Small language models (SLMs) can run on commodity hardware and support privacy-preserving, on-premises clinical deployment, but their medical explanations are often short and poorly structured compared with large language models. Recent supervised approaches such as Meerkat transfer chain-of-thought reasoning into 7B-8B backbones, yet their training objective does not directly target the style or organization of the generated rationales. Building on the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B backbone, we investigate whether a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) step can improve explanation structure without human preference labels. We apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with LoRA adaptation to 2000 Meerkat-derived medical prompts, guided by a simple self-supervised reward that favors longer, lexically diverse, and well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones. Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a stable increase in the average reward. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show that the RL-tuned model produces longer, more organized, multi-point explanations while preserving the underlying medical content. We discuss the promise and the limitations of self-rewarded RL for shaping the style of medical explanations.

title: Think Offline, Act in Real Time: Self-Improving Visual Game Agents through Code
abstract: Pre-trained models can read screens and reason about games, yet on an unfamiliar game, an agent still has to learn to play. We ask how an agent can self-improve on such a game from a few of its own attempts, in real-time visual games where the agent sees only the screen and the game keeps running while the agent thinks. We study two kinds of policy that can carry this improvement. In model as policy, a model selects actions during play; we adapt real-time chunking so that committed actions keep executing while the model reasons, and train a 2B controller for this interface. In code as policy, a model writes, tests, and revises a program between attempts, and the program acts during play. Across 170 GameWorld tasks, with at most eight one-minute executions per run, code as policy reaches 47.80% mean progress, against 30.90% for our trained controller, and leads in all five game categories. Improving the controller's weights on a single game, by contrast, yields only modest gains. These results favor letting a model think offline and storing what it learns in a program that acts in real time. Project repository: https://github.com/TabibitoQZP/SIGame

title: Towards Online Adaptive LLM-based Semantic Filtering
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) enable semantic filtering over unstructured documents using natural language predicates, but invoking an oracle LLM on every document incurs prohibitive monetary cost and online latency. Existing model-cascade approaches reduce this cost by using a lightweight proxy model to score each document and forwarding only uncertain documents to the oracle. However, their proxy models have limited generalization capability, and they typically adopt fixed sampling budgets for proxy training and threshold calibration, which insufficiently adapts to diverse online queries. To address this, we present OASIS, an online adaptive framework for LLM-based semantic filtering. OASIS combines a query-agnostic document similarity prior with query-adaptive online learning and sampling. In the offline phase, OASIS utilizes query-agnostic document similarity as a prior and constructs a document navigating spread-out graph (NSG) over document embeddings. For each online query, OASIS trains a query-conditioned graph attention network over the document NSG to obtain proxy scores through semi-supervised node classification. To allocate labels effectively, OASIS adopts density-aware active learning to explore uncertain score regions, selectively annotate informative documents, retrain the proxy, and stop early when additional labels are unlikely to improve the cascade. During threshold calibration, OASIS progressively samples an adaptively sized calibration set, adapting calibration cost to the query's score distribution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OASIS achieves a 1.75x-5.42x reduction in online latency and reduces the number of LLM-processed documents by 35%-75% relative to the state-of-the-art methods at an achieved accuracy of 0.9.

title: RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?
abstract: Improving the efficiency of training and inference infrastructure is a practical component of recursive self-improvement. Existing benchmarks for agent-driven optimization largely focus on individual software layers such as kernel, leaving unclear whether agents can deliver end-to-end performance gains under production workloads. We introduce RSIBench-Infra, a benchmark of 20 training and inference tasks spanning diverse model families and modalities, with deployments of up to 32 accelerators on NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Agents start from runnable baselines derived from official recipes and can modify the software stack across engine, kernel, and instruction levels. An OCI image-layer submission protocol captures these changes for reproducible deployment, while independent evaluation measures end-to-end performance under task-specific quality constraints. Across all task results, 66.2% exceed $1.10\times$ validated speedup. These results demonstrate that current agents can improve production-scale training and inference performance, but identifying effective optimization strategies and consistently translating local improvements into end-to-end gains remain challenging.

title: Semantic Context Handoff with On-Demand Evidence for Long-Horizon Agents
abstract: Traditional long-horizon LLM agents often hand off context through full-history prompting, retaining all previous action--observation interactions. As execution proceeds, this history keeps growing, increasing inference cost and potentially degrading accuracy. Existing methods control this growth by preserving compact conclusions while removing earlier observations, but doing so can discard evidence that later becomes relevant. We introduce Semantic Context Handoff (SCH), whose central abstraction is state--evidence separation: a compact semantic state carries the agent's current interpretation, while supporting action--observation evidence remains separately addressable and can re-enter context when later execution makes it relevant, without separate summarization or retrieval-model calls. Empirically, SCH improves long-horizon agent performance while substantially reducing context cost. In a controlled 150-task SWE-bench study, SCH's evidence recovery improves Pass@1 from $80.0\%$ to $86.9\%$ at essentially unchanged token use and execution time. In the complete-system comparison, SCH achieves 86.9% Pass@1 while using 43% fewer tokens and 41% less wall-clock time than the strongest baseline by task performance. Across models and benchmarks, SCH consistently reduces token use relative to full-history prompting while remaining competitive with or improving upon the evaluated baselines. Trajectory analysis confirms that SCH recovers evidence from substantially earlier parts of the interaction history rather than merely preserving a recent context window.

title: OpenKAGE: Open-Ended Lifelong Learning in the Open World via Knowledge-Sharing Agent-Group Evolution
abstract: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.

title: 3D GameDev Arena: Benchmarking Coding Agents That Plan, Build, and Playtest extreme Long-Horizon Browser Games
abstract: Coding agents now resolve repository issues and generate compact playable games, but whether they can build a large 3D game from scratch remains open. Such games tightly couple mechanics, scenes, assets, and interaction logic, and their quality rests on player enjoyment, which existing benchmarks rarely assess. Thus, we introduce 3D GameDev Arena, a first extreme long-horizon benchmark of 108 from-scratch game-development tasks across 14 genres. Given only a text specification and UI/UX reference images, a fully automated plan--implement--test--repair pipeline builds each task into a self-contained browser game. Runs average $\sim$1,000 LLM calls ; the longest uses 14,407 calls, 2.13B tokens, and 608 assets. Evaluation spans (1) objective code-level functional acceptance against the game specification, (2) agent-based QA and playtesting of 3D presentation and playability, and (3) blind pairwise Bradley-Terry human preference in a public arena. The preliminary findings indicate that long-horizon 3D game development remains far from solved, and code-level correctness alone does not dictate player preference. The public arena is hosted online.

title: Space-X: Self-Evolving Spatial Agents Weaving Clues into Evidence Chains
abstract: Spatial reasoning connects visual observations, geometric estimates, and linguistic decisions into a coherent derivation. Yet tool-augmented agents often acquire evidence without clear targets, combine outputs under inconsistent object or reference-frame semantics, and misjudge evidence sufficiency. Thus, more tools or calls do not reliably improve reasoning. We introduce Space-X, a spatial-reasoning framework that self-evolves toward complete, continuous evidence-chain construction. An Execution Agent acquires, associates, and judges evidence per problem using role-specific memory. A Control Agent diagnoses evidence-chain breaks from execution traces and jointly revises tools, interfaces, skills, memory organization, and decision rules. This loop co-evolves capability and evidence use: evidence needs guide capability development; usable results guide actions. Across multiple benchmarks, Space-X yields gains with four base models. Relative to baselines, GPT-6-sol improves answer accuracy on ViewSpatial and MMSI by 50.39% and 23.07%, respectively; Gemini-3.8-Flash gains 47.50% and 25.22% on these benchmarks. This provides a unified route from fragmented spatial clues to traceable, derivable answers.
affiliations: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences

title: SimplePro: A Simple Baseline for Proactive Video Understanding
abstract: Proactive video understanding requires vision-language models (VLMs) to decide not only what to answer as a video unfolds, but also when newly arrived evidence warrants a response and when to remain silent. Although modern VLMs excel at offline long-video understanding, they struggle in proactive streaming settings, leading prior work to introduce task-specific reinforcement learning or auxiliary triggering modules. We find that explicit reporting rules and structured streaming context substantially improve a frozen VLM's proactive response performance. We exploit this observation to build SIMPLEPRO, a training-free baseline for proactive video understanding. At each decision step, the model combines recent high-resolution frames, bounded historical observations, and prior answer records to determine whether new information warrants a response and, when needed, generate a concise answer. The system then filters consecutive duplicate answers while retaining the raw outputs as context for subsequent decisions. Without any parameter updates or auxiliary triggers, SIMPLEPRO with a 4B backbone consistently outperforms specialized proactive systems across OVO-Bench, StreamingBench-PO, and ProactiveVideoQA. SIMPLEPRO shows overall performance gains as backbone size increases from 2B to 32B. We hope this simple yet effective method will serve as a strong baseline for proactive video understanding, and we will release our code and inference pipeline to support future research.

title: EVA-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Evaluators for Judging Temporal Quality
abstract: Video evaluators play an important role in video generation, yet they miss motion defects, limiting the quality of generated videos. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has made strong progress in mathematics and coding, where explicit verifiers provide reliable feedback on a single goal. Video evaluation poses two difficulties for RSI: it has no verifier, and it must judge many dimensions at once, such as physics, smoothness and dynamics, where a gain on one can cost another. We introduce EVA-RSI, a multi-agent framework for exploring RSI under these two constraints. We build a fixed proxy exam with construction-defined targets by applying controlled changes to videos, such as temporal reversal and frame dropping. These edits supply supervision without human annotation. A small set of human-labeled real videos anchors the exam to human judgment. Each dimension has an LLM agent that proposes improvements. A leader agent coordinates the proposals, and a Nash bargaining rule selects updates that balance progress across dimensions. Humans design the exam, review candidate changes and revise the curriculum between stages. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, EVA-RSI improves motion evaluation, with the largest gain on smoothness, and the gains carry over to defect types never seen during the run. On the dynamics subsets of public benchmarks, our evaluator achieves the highest observed scores among 21 tested models. As an RL reward, it increases generated motion and earns human preference. A data-selection pipeline incorporating it also increases motion.

title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are pushing research toward semi-automation: ideas turn into preprints ever faster, and autoresearch pipelines add papers of uneven rigor. When a technique can be overtaken within months, citations arrive too late to tell which new papers deserve reading, so strong work goes unnoticed and newcomers lose their bearings. Yet from the day it appears, a preprint carries the track records of the people and institutions behind it. Established researchers guard their reputations and choose problems and collaborators with research taste, so their involvement tends to raise a paper's quality floor. Building on this signal, we present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight arXiv discovery tool that weights each paper's topical relevance by the reputation its authors and institutions stake on it. Author credit also diffuses by message passing along collaborations to surface rising stars, and institutions are profiled through the researchers they hold in each direction rather than by headcount. In a sealed test on 10,386 new papers, author credit doubled the chance of reaching the top tenth of early citations. As its library grows into a scholarly knowledge graph that research agents can query through a command-line interface (CLI), KnowMe also offers a promising literature entry point for future autoresearch and recursive self-improvement (RSI).

title: Communicative On-Policy Distillation: Distilling Black-Box Teacher Capabilities through Communication for Long-Horizon Tasks
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a powerful paradigm for improving language-model agents on long-horizon tasks, yet its conventional formulation relies on teacher logits that text-only black- box models do not expose. To address this limitation, we introduce Communicative On-Policy Distillation (COPD), which uses natural-language communication as a medium for distilling a stronger model's capabilities into a smaller student. During task execution, the student au- tonomously decides when to consult a black-box teacher and formulates open-ended natural- language requests without predefined question templates or intervention schedules. Successful student-teacher interactions are retained as privileged references to supervise fresh adviser-free student rollouts through on-policy self-distillation, jointly with task-reward reinforcement learning. On CAMG-II, COPD achieves 2.46 times the gain of the strongest black-box OPD baseline. The capabilities it learns through communication generalize to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, improving task success without adviser access.

title: Safe Personal RSI: Evaluating and Repairing Personal-Agent Updates
abstract: Kicker is a personal health assistant. Changes to an assistant's reusable instructions can improve task handling while changing what it discloses, which requests it follows, and how it reports actions. We study Safe Personal RSI, an update-evaluation component developed for Kicker. We restrict recursive self-improvement (RSI) to prompt updates, with model weights and runtime code fixed. The procedure tests proposed and current instructions, repeats failing cases, temporarily undoes changes to guide repairs, and checks safety and task performance before adoption. If no version passes, the current instructions stay in use. Our executable benchmark contains 29 email, calendar, health, and marketplace cases, with separate probes for authorization reuse, memory, and tool-output injection. Across three models and two deliberately risky edits, the procedure rejects 20 of 21 update attempts. In repair confirmation, an admitted GPT-5.6 Luna repair reduces attack violations from 10.7% to 0% and increases safe task completion from 89.7% to 100%; a broad handwritten authority rule matches these outcomes. Under stronger attacks, a repair transferred from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3-14B reduces violations from 69.0% to 17.9% and increases safe task completion from 19.5% to 64.4%. Separate runtime probes examine memory-entry deletion and identify missing local OAuth scope checks in the evaluated snapshot.
